newsitem.title: USA: NYC Council sees even bigger surplus than Hevesi.
newsitem.headline: NYC Council sees even bigger surplus than Hevesi.

text.p: The New York City Council predicted Wednesday the city's 1997 surplus would top $800 million, about $100 million more than forecast by the City Comptroller, Alan Hevesi, who looks for a record windfall.
"The challenge we face now is how to invest these resources to best prepare the city for continued economic growth," said City Council Speaker, Peter Vallone, a Democrat, in prepared remarks.
The Council noted that in March, it had said additional revenues would produce a $630 million surplus, but said it had not accounted for underspending by agencies.

Finance Chair Herbert Berman attributed most of the windfall to Wall Street's strong performance, and made it plain the Democrat-led council will try to get the Giuliani Administration to direct city agencies to spend all their money. "We are seeing, at the state and city level, what can only be described as a remarkable performance by the New York City financial services sector," he said, in prepared remarks.
He added: "A great concern to all council members is gross agency underspending in areas that are underserved, especially in the area of homeless services."
A spokeswoman for the Republican mayor was not immediately available to comment.

Saying the city still needs to solve long-term, structural budget problems, the Council honed in on four main points: expanding its economic base through targetted tax cuts, continuing investments in education, funding for "improved service delivery," and creating a Rainy Day Fund, which could be tapped if the economy turned down. Such a fund would have to be approved both by Giuliani and Albany.
